units.title: Abeceda · The alphabet
units.intro: The Slovak alphabet has 46 letters. Tap each one to hear how it's said: that's how Slovaks spell words out loud, for example your name or email on the phone. Vowels (and ĺ, ŕ) are simply said as their sound; most consonants have a short name ending in -é (bé, cé) or starting with e- (el, em, es).

items.sk: a e i o u y
á é í ó ú ý
b c č d ď f g h
ch j k l ĺ ľ m n ň
items.en: ch to ň (ch is one letter)

items.sk: p q r ŕ s š t ť
v w x z ž dz dž

units.title: Vowels & stress
units.intro: Slovak is spelled the way it sounds. Learn the sounds once and you can read anything. Vowels are short and pure, with no English-style glide (Slovak o never turns into "ow"). And stress is always on the first syllable.
units.logic: Fixed stress is a gift: once you know where a word starts, you know where to stress it, so you never have to memorise it word by word.
units.fr: French stresses the last syllable of a phrase; Slovak always stresses the first. Same kind of rule, opposite end.

items.en: both are a short 'ee', exactly the same sound
items.explain: i and y sound identical. The difference is only spelling (and it decides whether d, t, n, l before it are soft, which comes later).
No exceptions: BRA-ti-sla-va, A-me-ri-ka, TE-le-fón. English speakers tend to stress the middle (a-ME-ri-ka), so watch out for that.

units.title: Ahoj! Greetings
units.intro: Slovak has two words for "you": ty for friends, family and kids, and vy for strangers, elders and formal situations. With your boyfriend's parents, start with vy until they offer ty.
units.logic: Formality is built into the verb: ty forms end in -š (máš), vy forms in -te (máte). Hear the ending and you know the relationship.
units.fr: ty / vy works exactly like tu / vous, including vy for one person you respect. Prosím covers s'il vous plaît, je vous en prie and pardon ? all at once.

items.note: Literally "good day". Use it in shops and with anyone older.
Super versatile: please, you're welcome, here you go, and "pardon?"
In casual speech you'll often hear just "hej".

units.title: Long vowels
units.intro: The accent mark ´ (called dĺžeň) means hold the vowel about twice as long. It does not mean stress, and the length can change a word's meaning completely.

items.sk: á é í ý ó ú
items.en: same vowel, held twice as long
a long vowel can sit in an unstressed syllable
items.explain: In te-le-fón and ka-ma-rát the stress is still on the first syllable, but the last vowel is held long. Get both right and you'll sound very natural.

units.title: Háček sounds
units.intro: The little hook ˇ (called mäkčeň) turns hissy sounds into hushy ones. These four are easy for English speakers, because you already have them.
units.fr: You already know these sounds: š is French ch (chat), ž is French j (je), and č is the tch in tchèque. Slovak simply gives each sound its own letter.

units.title: Zoznámenie · Meeting people
units.intro: Some words change depending on who is speaking. A woman says Som Američanka, a man says Som Američan. Where it matters, these lessons use the version for a woman speaking.
units.fr: Volám sa Anna is word for word je m'appelle Anna: sa is French se. And like French, Slovak has years: Mám tridsať rokov = j'ai trente ans.

items.note: Swap in your own name!

items.sk: Hovorím po anglicky a po francúzsky.

units.title: Byť · To be
units.intro:
The most important verb. Slovak usually drops the pronoun, because the verb already says who: Som doma means "I'm at home".
jasomI am
tysiyou are
on / ona / onojehe / she / it is
mysmewe are
vysteyou are (formal / plural)
onisúthey are
Negative: put nie in front, as a separate word: nie som, nie je.
units.logic: Pronouns are optional because the verb ending already says who: som can only mean "I am". Slovaks add ja, ty… only for emphasis.
units.fr: byť is être, and just as irregular: som / si / je ≈ suis / es / est. Negation is easier: just nie in front, no ne … pas sandwich.

units.title: Nerozumiem · When you're lost
units.intro: The phrases that keep a conversation alive when you don't follow. Slovaks are delighted that you're trying, and will happily slow down or repeat if you ask.
units.logic: Nerozumiem is ne + rozumiem: "not" is glued straight onto the verb. Same with neviem (I don't know).
units.fr: Pomalšie, prosím = Plus lentement, s'il vous plaît. Čo to znamená? = Qu'est-ce que ça veut dire ?

items.sk: Ako sa to povie po slovensky?
items.en: How do you say that in Slovak?

units.title: Special vowels
units.intro: Slovak has a few vowels English doesn't: ä, ô, and the gliding pairs ia, ie, iu.

items.en: officially 'a' as in 'cat', but most people just say 'e'
start with a 'y' sound: 'ya', 'ye' (and the rare 'yu')

units.title: Rodina · Family
units.intro: Every Slovak noun is masculine, feminine or neuter. The ending usually tells you which: consonant → masculine, -a → feminine, -o / -e → neuter. "My" changes to match: môj brat, moja mama, moje dieťa.
units.logic: The ending usually tells you the gender, so you learn the word and get its gender for free: consonant = masculine, -a = feminine, -o / -e = neuter.
units.fr: Like French, every noun has a gender and "my" agrees: môj / moja like mon / ma. Slovak adds a third gender (neuter), but no le / la to memorise.

items.note: Ends in -o but masculine, because it's a man. Meaning beats ending.

items.sk: Moja rodina žije v štáte Maine.

units.title: Soft consonants
units.intro: ď ť ň ľ are made by pressing the middle of your tongue against the roof of your mouth. Say "yes" and notice where your tongue is. That's the spot. This is the most Slovak-sounding part of Slovak.
units.fr: ň is the French gn in montagne or champagne. ľ is close to the li in million said quickly, as one sound.

items.en: a 'd' with a 'y' squeezed in, like British 'during'
a 't' with a 'y' squeezed in, like British 'tune'

items.sk: de te ne le · di ti ni li
items.en: soft automatically before e and i
items.explain: Before e and i, the letters d, t, n, l are usually pronounced soft, with no háček needed: deti sounds like "ďeťi". Before y they stay hard. Exceptions: ten (that), jeden (one), and most foreign words like telefón.

units.title: Jedlo · Food & drink
units.intro: When you order or want something, feminine words ending in -a switch to -u: káva → Prosím si kávu. That's your first taste of Slovak cases. No need to master it yet, just notice it.
units.logic: Slovak has no articles. Káva means "coffee", "a coffee" and "the coffee". The job articles do in French is done by context and word endings.
units.fr: Mám hlad = j'ai faim, exactly. Both languages have hunger.

items.note: Literally "I have hunger."
Essential at a Slovak grandma's table. (It may not work.)

units.title: I want, I have, I see
units.intro:
This is your first real case, the accusative. When a noun is the thing you want, have or see, its ending can change:
f-a → -ukáva → Chcem kávu.
m person or animal+ -abrat → Mám brata.
m thingno changeChcem čaj.
nno changeChcem pivo.
"That" changes too: tá žena → Vidím tú ženu.
units.logic: Endings mark who does what, so word order is free: Mám brata and Brata mám mean the same, the second just stresses "a brother".
units.fr: French does this only with pronouns: il voit Pierre → il le voit. Slovak marks every noun, the way French marks le / lui.

items.note: pes → psa: the e drops out. A few short words do this.

units.title: c, ch, h, j, r, dz
units.intro: A few letters look familiar but sound different from English. These are the classic beginner traps.
units.fr: Careful: Slovak ch is not French ch. It's the rough sound in German Bach. And unlike French, h is always pronounced. j is the French y in yaourt.

items.en: a soft, voiced 'h' from the throat
a tapped or rolled 'r', like Spanish

units.title: Doma · At home
units.intro: Watch for the gender exceptions here: posteľ ends in a consonant but is feminine, and dvere (door) is always plural, even for one door.

units.title: Ten, tá, to · Gender in action
units.intro:
Words that describe a noun take its gender. Masculine words end in -ý, feminine in -á, neuter in -é. "That/the" works the same way.
mten dobrý brat
ftá dobrá sestra
nto dobré pivo
"My" follows the same pattern: môj, moja, moje.
units.logic: Words that describe a noun copy its gender, so you can tell what belongs together even in a long sentence.
units.fr: Agreement works like French adjectives (petit / petite → malý / malá), but Slovak always puts the adjective before the noun. ten / tá / to behave like ce / cette, not le / la.

units.title: Where? · v, na
units.intro:
After v (in) and na (on / at), place names change their ending, usually to -e or -i:
Bratislava→ v Bratislave
obchod→ v obchode
práca→ v práci
letisko→ na letisku
Some places use na instead of v, which you just have to learn: na stanici, na letisku, and na Slovensku (but v Amerike).
units.fr: Choosing v or na is as arbitrary as en France, au Canada, à Paris: learn each place together with its preposition.

items.en: The key is on the table.

variants.en: The phone is on the table.
The key is in the car.

items.en: The pharmacy is on the square.

units.title: Clusters & endings
units.intro: Two last things and you can read Slovak: r and l can act as vowels, and sounds at the end of a word lose their "buzz".

items.en: words with no vowel at all
items.explain: In vlk and krk, the r or l carries the syllable. Just glide straight through, and don't add an 'uh'.
At the end of a word, buzzy sounds lose their buzz: chlieb sounds like "chliep", hrad like "hrat", muž like "muš". Spelling doesn't change, only sound.

items.en: at the end of a syllable, v sounds like a short 'w'

units.title: Čísla · Numbers
units.intro: "One" and "two" change with gender: jeden brat, jedna sestra, jedno pivo · dva (m) / dve (f, n). From three up, no changes.

items.note: Literally "How many years do you have?"

units.title: Čas · Time & days
units.intro: Days of the week aren't capitalised in Slovak. Most are simply named by number: utorok (2nd), štvrtok (4th), piatok (5th). Streda means "middle".

units.title: Questions & saying no
units.intro: To say "don't", glue ne- onto the front of the verb: mám → nemám, chcem → nechcem. The only exception is byť: nie som, nie je. For a yes/no question, keep the same words and raise your voice at the end: Máš čas?
units.logic: Negation glues onto the verb (ne-), so a negative sentence is often a single word: Nechcem.
units.fr: ne- is French ne … pas squeezed into one syllable. Yes/no questions work like spoken French: Tu as le temps ? = Máš čas?, same words, rising voice.

units.title: Present tense · What I do
units.intro:
Good news: every "I" form ends in -m (except som). Verbs follow three main patterns, and only the vowel changes:
volať (call)robiť (do)písať (write)
javolámrobímpíšem
tyvolášrobíšpíšeš
on/onavolárobípíše
myvolámerobímepíšeme
vyvoláterobítepíšete
onivolajúrobiapíšu
units.logic: The ending carries the person, which is why the pronoun can be dropped. Learn the six endings once and they work for almost every verb.
units.fr: Same principle as French conjugation, except every ending is pronounced. Handy anchors: -me ≈ -ons (robíme = nous faisons), -te ≈ -ez (robíte = vous faites).

items.en: What do you want to do? (informal)
items.note: chcieť (to want) is irregular: chcem, chceš, chce, chceme, chcete, chcú.

units.title: Láska · Feelings & love
units.intro: Feelings change form with the speaker: a woman says Som šťastná and Mám ťa rada, a man says Som šťastný and Mám ťa rád. These lessons use the version for a woman speaking.
units.logic: With feelings that happen to you, Slovak puts you in the "to whom" form: Je mi zima is literally "to me it is cold".
units.fr: French uses avoir (j'ai froid); Slovak says "it is cold to me". Same idea as ça me plaît: the thing affects you.

items.en: I really like you / love you. (woman speaking)
items.note: Warm and a little softer than Ľúbim ťa. Used with family too.
Literally "You are missing to me."
Literally "It is winter to me."
Literally "little gold".

items.en: I'm looking forward to seeing you.

units.title: Want, can, must
units.intro:
Three helper verbs plus a second verb in the -ť form (the infinitive):
chcieťChcem ísť.I want to go.
môcťMôžem ísť.I can go.
musieťMusím ísť.I have to go.
vedieťViem variť.I know how to cook.
units.fr: vedieť vs môcť is exactly savoir vs pouvoir: Viem plávať = je sais nager (a skill), Môžem plávať = je peux nager (I'm able or allowed right now).

variants.en: I want to go to the shop.
Can you write it down for me? (formal)

items.en: Do you want to go out? (informal)

items.note: Use vedieť (not môcť) for skills: Viem plávať = I can swim.

units.title: Vonku · Out and about
units.intro: Enough to get around a Slovak town, order in a café and pay. In shops, always greet with Dobrý deň when you walk in.

units.title: Past tense · What I did
units.intro:
One of the easiest parts of Slovak. Take the infinitive, drop -ť, and add an ending for gender:
robiť →robil (he)robila (she)robili (they)
For "I" and "you", add som / si: Robila som = I did (said by a woman), Robil som = I did (said by a man). For "we" and "you (formal)", add sme / ste with the -li form.
units.logic: One form for all past actions: drop -ť, add -l / -la / -li. The ending agrees with who did it, so the past tense always tells you their gender.
units.fr: It's the passé composé with être-style agreement: elle est allée / il est allé. Slovak does it with every verb: bola som / bol som. som works like the auxiliary.

items.en: What did you do? (to a man)

items.note: jesť (to eat) is irregular: jedol, jedla, jedli.

units.title: Lekárka · At the hospital
units.intro: In Slovak healthcare, always use vy with patients and address them as pán / pani + surname. Female surnames end in -ová or -á: pán Novák, pani Nováková. Job titles have feminine forms, so you are a lekárka and a psychiatrička.

items.note: A male doctor is lekár.
A male psychiatrist is psychiater.
Usually just sestra, the same word as "sister".
Also means "recipe".
Nech sa páči: "please, go ahead / come in / here you are".

units.title: The first conversation
units.intro: Opening an interview. These are all formal (vy) questions. Notice the endings: -te marks the formal "you" in verbs, like cítite, prichádzate, rozumiete.

items.note: Literally "What are you coming with?". The standard opener in Slovak clinics.

items.en: How long has this been going on?

units.title: Nálada · Mood & emotions
units.intro: Many emotion words are feminine nouns ending in -osť (úzkosť, beznádejnosť), like English "-ness". Patients will often describe feelings with Cítim sa… (I feel…) or Je mi… (Je mi smutno, "I feel sad").

items.en: Do you feel sad? (to a man)
items.note: To a woman: Cítite sa smutná?

items.en: Does anything still bring you joy?

units.title: Spánok · Sleep, appetite, focus
units.intro: The biological symptoms. Past-tense questions to patients use the -li ste form for both men and women: Schudli ste? (Have you lost weight?).

items.en: Do you wake up at night?
Are you able to fall asleep?

items.note: What a patient might say. A woman says: Som stále unavená.

items.sk: Pracujem aj s pacientmi s poruchami príjmu potravy.
items.en: I also work with patients with eating disorders.

units.title: Assessment & risk
units.intro: Screening questions, including risk. These are worth knowing word-for-word. A gentle lead-in like Musím sa vás opýtať… (I have to ask you…) is common in Slovak too.

items.sk: Uvažovali ste o tom, že by ste si ublížili?
items.en: Have you thought about hurting yourself?
Do you hear voices that others don't hear?
Are you allergic to any medications?
How much alcohol do you drink?

items.sk: Má niekto v rodine psychické problémy?
items.en: Does anyone in your family have mental health problems?

units.title: Liečba · Treatment
units.intro: Explaining a plan. Instructions to patients use the formal imperative, ending in -te: Užívajte (take), Zavolajte (call), Príďte (come).

items.sk: Účinok nastúpi o dva až štyri týždne.
items.en: It takes two to four weeks to start working.
I'll see you in two weeks.

items.sk: Ak sa budete cítiť horšie, zavolajte.

units.title: Kto je to? · Who's that?
units.intro: Spotting people across the room. ho = him, ju = her: Poznáš ho? / Poznáš ju?. And the golden rule of Slovak parties: Neotáčaj sa! (Don't turn around!)

items.sk: Kto je tá žena v červených šatách?
items.en: Who's the woman in the red dress?
The tall one by the bar.

units.title: Ako vyzerá · Looks
units.intro: Classic party commentary uses the past tense, so the ending tells you who you're talking about: Schudla (she lost weight) vs Schudol (he lost weight).

items.en: Did you see her dress? (to a woman)

units.title: Povaha · Personality
units.intro: Adjectives are given in the masculine form (-ý). For a woman, switch to -á: vtipný → vtipná, žiarlivý → žiarlivá.

units.title: Vzťahy · Who's with whom
units.intro: Slovak has two words for "married": a man is ženatý (he has a žena), a woman is vydatá. Couples do things with sa: rozišli sa (they broke up), berú sa (they're getting married).

items.note: Literally "She is pleasing to him."

units.title: Počula si? · Did you hear?
units.intro: The essential gossip word is vraj: "apparently / supposedly / they say". Vraj dostal výpoveď = Apparently he got fired. It lets you pass on news without vouching for it.

items.en: I didn't tell you anything. (woman speaking)

units.title: Pst, ide sem! · Cover story
units.intro: When the subject of the gossip walks over, switch smoothly to small talk. A woman says Rada ťa vidím, a man says Rád ťa vidím.

units.title: Sviatky · Holidays & wishes
units.intro: Slovaks celebrate meniny (name days) almost as much as birthdays. Every day of the calendar has a name, and if it's yours, expect flowers and a toast. The big Christmas celebration is on the evening of the 24th, Štedrý večer.

items.note: The all-purpose wish: birthdays, name days, New Year.
Literally "the generous evening". Carp, potato salad and kapustnica (sauerkraut soup).
Literally "the great night".
Boys splash girls with water (sometimes a whole bucket). Girls give them painted eggs or a shot. Yes, really.

units.title: Svadba · The wedding
units.intro: Slovak weddings go all night. Around midnight comes the čepčenie: the bride's veil is replaced with a married woman's cap, while the women sing.

items.note: Literally "witness". The maid of honor is svedkyňa.

units.title: Na zdravie! · Toasts
units.intro: When you clink glasses in Slovakia, look the other person in the eyes. Legend says otherwise it's seven years of bad luck (in bed). The hosts will keep refilling, so learn the polite ways to slow down.

items.note: The one excuse every Slovak host accepts.

items.sk: Som šťastná, keď mám plný dom hostí.
items.en: I'm happiest with a house full of guests. (woman)

units.title: Počasie · Weather & seasons
units.intro: Slovak weather verbs need no "it": Prší (it's raining), Sneží (it's snowing). And zima means both "winter" and "cold", so Je zima means "it's cold".
units.fr: Prší = il pleut, but without the il: Slovak doesn't need an empty subject.

units.title: Na trhu · At the market
units.intro: After an amount (kilo, kúsok, veľa) the noun takes a new ending, so jablká becomes kilo jabĺk. Learn it as a chunk for now; Gramatika 2 explains why.

items.en: No, thanks, I have my own.

units.title: Môj deň · Daily routine
units.intro: Times of day use o + an ordinal: o siedmej (at seven), o šiestej (at six). Meals have their own verbs too: raňajkovať, "to have breakfast".

items.note: An important negotiation in any Slovak household.

items.en: I love having friends over for dinner.
In the evening I like watching true crime series.

units.title: Telefón · Calls, texts & spelling
units.intro: Slovaks answer the phone with Haló? or just Prosím? and hang up with a quick Pa pa! (bye-bye). Napíš mi means "write to me", which these days means "text me". On the phone you'll also need to spell things: letters are said the way you learned in the alphabet lesson, and because i and y sound the same, Slovaks say mäkké i (soft i) or tvrdé y (hard y).

items.en: I'll be there in ten minutes.

units.title: Z, do, bez · Of, from, without
units.intro:
The genitive case answers "of what / from where". It comes after do (to/into), z (from), bez (without), od (from someone), u (at someone's), and after amounts like pohár, kúsok, veľa.
f-a → -y (-e after soft letters)voda → pohár vody
m thing+ -uobchod → do obchodu
m person+ -aotec → auto otca
n-o → -amlieko → bez mlieka
units.logic: The genitive marks "of": a part of something, where something comes from, or what's missing.
units.fr: Think of it as French de: pohár vody = un verre d'eau, kúsok chleba = un morceau de pain, bez cukru = sans sucre, and u mamy = chez maman, exactly.

items.note: Revúca declines like an adjective (-á → -ej).
chlieb → chleba: the ie shortens. Irregular, but very common.

items.en: I have a lot of work.

items.note: otec → otca: the e drops out, just like pes → psa.

units.title: S, pod, pred · With
units.intro:
The instrumental case means "with" or "by means of". You already know one: platiť kartou. It also follows pod (under), nad (above), pred (in front of), za (behind), medzi (between).
f-a → -ous mamou
m n→ -oms bratom, autom
Before words starting with s, z, š or ž, s becomes so: so sestrou.
units.logic: The instrumental answers "with what / with whom / by what means". One ending does the work of a preposition.
units.fr: s mamou = avec maman, autom = en voiture, kartou = par carte. Where French needs en or par, Slovak often needs only the ending.

items.en: The key is under the table.
Let's meet in front of the cinema.
I like doing puzzles with friends.
My friends and I swap books.

units.title: Komu? · To whom
units.intro:
The dative is for the person something goes to. You've been using it since day one: Je mi zima, Chýbaš mi, Páči sa mi.
mito menámto us
tito youvámto you (formal)
mu / jejto him / herimto them
Nouns: feminine -e (mame), masculine people -ovi (bratovi).
units.logic: The dative marks the person something goes to or happens to: giving, telling, liking, feeling.
units.fr: It's the French indirect object, à quelqu'un: mu / jej / im = lui / lui / leur. Páči sa mi is literally ça me plaît.

items.note: fandiť (to cheer for) takes the dative: who are you cheering to?

units.title: Budúci čas · The future
units.intro:
Two ways to talk about the future:
budem + infinitiveongoing: Budem pracovať. I'll be working.
a "completed" verbits present form already means future: Urobím to. I'll get it done.
Completed verbs usually just add a prefix: robiť → urobiť, písať → napísať, volať → zavolať. Never combine them: budem urobiť is the classic learner mistake.
units.logic: Slovak verbs come in pairs: one for the process (robiť, to be doing), one for the result (urobiť, to get it done). The "done" verb in present form points to the future.
units.fr: Aspect will feel familiar: the process verb ≈ imparfait (ongoing, repeated), the result verb ≈ passé composé (completed). Budem robiť works like futur proche: je vais faire.

items.en: I'll call you in the evening.

variants.en: I'll text you in the evening.

items.en: What are we going to do?

units.title: Množné číslo · More than one
units.intro:
Plurals depend on gender:
m people-ištudent → študenti
m things-ydom → domy
f-y / -ežena → ženy
n-á / -iaauto → autá
With 2, 3 and 4, use this plural (dve kávy). From 5 up, the noun shifts again (päť minút).
units.fr: From five upwards Slovak switches to the "of" form, a bit like French beaucoup de: päť minút is literally "five of minutes".

items.en: The women are in the kitchen.

items.note: priateľ → priatelia is irregular.

units.title: Lepší, najlepší · Better, the best
units.intro:
Comparatives end in -ší or -ejší; the superlative adds naj-. "Than" is ako. The most common ones are irregular, just like in English:
dobrýlepšínajlepší
zlýhoršínajhorší
veľkýväčšínajväčší
malýmenšínajmenší
Like other adjectives they change with gender: lepší / lepšia / lepšie.
units.fr: Irregular in the same places as French: dobrý → lepší like bon → meilleur. naj- works like le / la plus, and ako = que: väčšia ako = plus grande que.

items.note: But you're doing it anyway.

units.title: U lekára · At the doctor
units.intro: This time you're the patient. Pain in Slovak is something that happens to you: Bolí ma hlava, literally "the head hurts me".
units.logic: In Bolí ma hlava, the body part is the subject (hlava) and you are the object (ma = me). So it's Bolia ma nohy (my legs hurt), with the verb agreeing with the legs.
units.fr: French uses a fixed formula, j'ai mal à la tête. Slovak flips it around: "the head hurts me". But Mám horúčku = j'ai de la fièvre: both have a fever.

items.en: I have an appointment at ten. (woman)
I need something for the pain.

units.title: Oblečenie · Clothes & shopping
units.intro: Colours are adjectives, so they change with the noun: modrý kabát, modrá sukňa, modré šaty. The words below are in the masculine form.
units.fr: Colours agree just like in French (bleu / bleue → modrý / modrá), but in Slovak they come before the noun: červená sukňa = une jupe rouge. Len sa pozerám = je regarde seulement.

items.note: Always plural, like dvere.

items.en: Do you have it in another size?

variants.en: Do you have it in another colour?
Do you have it in red?

units.title: Cestovanie · Travel
units.intro: Tickets and trains use what you learned in Gramatika 2: do + the "of" form for where you're going (do Bratislavy), and z for where from.
units.fr: Spiatočný lístok = un aller-retour. Ako sa dostanem na stanicu? works like comment je vais à la gare ?, with sa just as in se rendre.

items.en: How do I get to the station?

units.title: Bývanie · Home & housing
units.intro: Rooms, appliances and everyday problems. Floors are counted like in Europe: the ground floor is prízemie, so na treťom poschodí is the American fourth floor.
units.fr: Floors work like in France: prízemie = rez-de-chaussée, and na treťom poschodí = au troisième étage.

items.note: A woman neighbour is suseda.

items.en: We live on the third floor.
Could you come and fix the washing machine?

units.title: Sa a si · Reflexive verbs
units.intro: Many Slovak verbs travel with a little word: sa (oneself) or si (for / to oneself). It stays the same for every person: učím sa, učíš sa, učí sa. Some verbs only exist with it: báť sa (to be afraid), smiať sa (to laugh).
units.logic: sa = the action turns back on you (obliecť sa, to dress oneself). si = you do it for yourself (kúpiť si, to buy for oneself). That's why ordering food uses si: Dám si kávu, "I'll give myself a coffee".
units.fr: sa is French se: je m'appelle = volám sa, je me dépêche = ponáhľam sa. Simpler, though: one form for all persons, where French changes me / te / se / nous / vous. si is the me in je me suis acheté une robe = kúpila som si šaty.

items.note: Careful: se is Czech, not Slovak.

items.en: I bought myself a new dress. (woman)

units.title: Kondicionál · Would
units.intro: "Would" is easy: the past form + by. Robila by som = I would do (woman). It's also the polite way to ask: Chcela by som… (I'd like…), Mohli by ste…? (Could you…?).
units.logic: by never changes; the past form shows the gender as usual. "If" is keby, and it already contains the by: Keby som mala čas, prišla by som.
units.fr: It's the conditionnel: je voudrais = chcela by som, the polite way to order in both languages. In "if" sentences French uses the imparfait after si, but Slovak uses the conditional in both halves: si j'avais le temps, je viendrais = keby som mala čas, prišla by som.

variants.en: I'd like a glass of wine. (woman)
Could you call me a taxi? (formal)
variants.sk: Mohli by ste mi zavolať taxík?

items.en: What would you like to do? (to a man)

items.sk: Keby som mala čas, prišla by som.
items.en: If I had time, I would come. (woman)

items.sk: Bolo by fajn ísť do Tatier.
items.en: It would be nice to go to the Tatras.

items.sk: Na tvojom mieste by som to nerobila.
items.en: If I were you, I wouldn't do it. (woman)
Would you come with me? (to a woman)

units.title: Ísť a chodiť · Coming and going
units.intro: Slovak splits "to go" in two: ísť for one trip, now or heading somewhere (idem), and chodiť for going regularly (chodím). Prefixes add the direction: prí- (arrive), od- (leave), vy- (go out / get off), pre- (cross).
units.logic: The future of ísť is special: pôjdem, pôjdeš, pôjde…, never budem ísť. Prefixed verbs (prídem, odídem) work like the "done" verbs from Gramatika 2: their present form means the future.
units.fr: French has one aller; Slovak distinguishes je vais (right now: idem) from j'y vais tous les jours (habit: chodím). Prefixes do what French does with separate verbs: prísť = arriver / venir, odísť = partir, vojsť = entrer, vyjsť = sortir.

items.en: I go to work every day.

variants.en: I go to the gym every day.
Every Sunday I go to Grandma's.

items.en: I'm just going to the shop.
Do you go to the gym? (informal)

items.note: The standard way to invite someone in. To a friend: Poď ďalej.

items.en: We'll get off at the next stop.

units.title: Myslím, že… · Saying what you think
units.intro: Small linking words let you say more than one thing at a time: že (that), lebo (because), ale (but), preto (so), keď (when), aby (so that), či (whether).
units.logic: Slovak always puts a comma before že, lebo, keď, aby, či: the comma marks where a new idea starts. And aby takes the past form, like the conditional: aby som rozumela.
units.fr: Myslím, že máš pravdu = je pense que tu as raison, and both languages have right (mať pravdu = avoir raison). že = que, lebo = parce que, ale = mais, či = si (whether). aby = pour que, and like pour que + subjonctif, it needs a special verb form.

variants.en: I think it's a good idea.
variants.sk: Myslím, že je to dobrý nápad.

items.sk: Podľa mňa je to dobrý nápad.
items.en: In my opinion it's a good idea.
I won't come because I'm ill. (woman)

variants.en: I won't come because I'm tired. (woman)
I won't come because I have to work.

items.en: It was raining, so we stayed at home.

items.sk: Keď budem mať čas, zavolám ti.
items.en: When I have time, I'll call you.

items.sk: Učím sa po slovensky, aby som rozumela tvojej rodine.
items.en: I'm learning Slovak so that I can understand your family. (woman)
I don't know whether he'll come.

units.title: Varenie · Cooking
units.intro: Ingredients, kitchen things, and how recipes talk to you: in short, friendly commands.
units.logic: A command comes straight from the ty form: drop the ending and you have it. miešaš → miešaj, pridáš → pridaj, nakrájaš → nakrájaj.
units.fr: Recipes give orders in both languages: pridaj = ajoute, miešaj = mélange, nakrájaj = coupe.

items.note: Feminine, even though it ends in a consonant.

units.title: V reštaurácii · At a restaurant
units.intro: Paying the Slovak way: when the waiter brings the bill, you don't leave coins on the table. You say the total you want to pay, tip included (about 5–10%). For a 27-euro bill: Dajte mi z toho tridsať, "take thirty out of it".
units.fr: Spolu alebo zvlášť? = ensemble ou séparément ? And just like ordering in France, Dám si… / Prosím si… is how you say what you'll have.

items.note: A waitress is čašníčka.

items.en: Do you have a free table?
Make it thirty. (paying, with a tip)

units.title: Pri stole · At the table
units.intro: Family meals. Lunch (obed) is traditionally the main hot meal of the day, often with soup first. At Slovak tables, leaving food on your plate can read as "I didn't like it", so take small portions.
units.fr: Nalej mi vody = verse-moi de l'eau: here the "of" form means "some", just like French du / de l'.

items.en: Who's going to wash the dishes?

units.title: Doprava · Traffic & driving
units.intro: Driving, trams and traffic jams. Fun fact: doprava means both "traffic / transport" and "to the right".
units.logic: vpravo / vľavo say where something is (on the right). doprava / doľava say where to (turn to the right). Same pattern as doma (at home) vs domov (home-wards).
units.fr: vodičský preukaz (colloquially vodičák) = le permis. Zabočte doprava = tournez à droite.

items.en: We need to fill up the tank.

units.title: Vybavovačky · Errands
units.intro: Vybavovačky means "running errands": the post office, the bank, offices, forms. At a counter or a doctor's waiting room, Slovaks ask Kto je posledný? (who's last?) and then simply wait behind that person.
units.fr: Vybavovačky ≈ faire des démarches. And note účet means both "bill" (l'addition) and "bank account" (le compte).

items.en: I'd like to send a parcel. (woman)
Do I have to fill in a form?
I'll come and pick it up tomorrow.

units.title: Koníčky · Hobbies
units.intro: What people do after work. Slovaks are serious hikers (turistika), and in winter half the country is on skis.
units.logic: Rada (she) / rád (he) + a verb = to like doing it: Rada čítam "I like reading". A sport is played straight: hrám tenis. An instrument takes na + the "where" form: hrám na klavíri, na gitare.
units.fr: Like French, sports and music take different little words: hrať futbal = jouer au foot, hrať na klavíri = jouer du piano.

items.note: Literally "little horse", the same picture as the English hobby-horse.
Not tourism! Turistika is walking in the hills.

items.en: What are you doing at the weekend?

items.note: hory → do hôr: "of the mountains", with a long ô.
Literally "it entertains me": the thing is the subject, you're the object.

items.en: Are you coming to the cinema with us?

units.title: Hodiny a dátumy · Times & dates
units.intro: Half past three is "half of four" in Slovak: pol štvrtej. You count toward the coming hour.
units.logic: "At" a time is o + an ordinal: o jednej, o druhej, o tretej (the hour is feminine, hodina). Dates use ordinals too: prvého mája "on the first of May".
units.fr: The months will look familiar: január, február, marec = janvier, février, mars. And the day comes first, as in French: 1. mája = le 1er mai.

items.note: Also "the moon": months were counted by it.
Literally "half of the fourth".
Literally "a quarter toward five".
Three quarters of the way toward six.
1 May is also the Slovak day of love: couples kiss under a blossoming tree.

items.en: Where were you born? (to a woman)

units.title: V práci · At work
units.intro: Office talk. Titles still matter at work (pán doktor, pani inžinierka), and so does the morning coffee.
units.logic: Events take na, buildings take v: som na porade (in a meeting), na obede, na dovolenke, but som v kancelárii, v nemocnici.
units.fr: Same Latin roots: kolega = collègue, kancelária ≈ chancellerie, projekt = projet.

items.note: A woman colleague is kolegyňa.
A woman boss is šéfka.

items.en: I've got a lot on today.

items.note: služba is a hospital shift; in a factory it's zmena.

units.title: Dovolenka · Holidays
units.intro: A Slovak summer means the Croatian coast (Slovakia has no sea of its own), the High Tatras, or the family chata, a cottage in the hills.
units.logic: Being somewhere vs going there: som pri mori (at the sea) but idem k moru (to the sea); som na horách but idem na hory. The ending tells you which.
units.fr: dovolenka = les vacances, and a chata is close to a chalet.

items.note: Many families have one, for weekends and long summers.

items.en: I still have to pack my suitcase.
Where are you going in summer? (to a couple)

items.note: kúpať sa: to bathe, to swim for fun. Plávať is swimming as a sport.

items.en: Do you have a free room?
In winter we go to the Tatras.
items.note: Tatry → do Tatier, like hory → do hôr.

units.title: Vid · Doing vs done
units.intro: The big A2 idea. Most Slovak verbs come in pairs: one for an action in progress, one for a finished result.
units.logic: Píšem: I'm writing (in progress). Napíšem: I'll write it (and finish). A "done" verb in the present form means the future: urobím "I'll do it". The pair usually differs by a prefix: robiť → urobiť, písať → napísať, čítať → prečítať, variť → uvariť. Ongoing future uses budem: budem čakať; a "done" verb never does.
units.fr: It's the imparfait vs passé composé split, built into the verb itself: čítala som ≈ je lisais, prečítala som ≈ j'ai lu (jusqu'au bout).

items.en: I'm writing an email right now.

items.note: "Done" verb + present ending = future.

items.en: I was reading all evening. (she says)
I read the whole book, cover to cover. (she says)

items.note: Habits are never "done": vždy kupujem.

items.en: I'll buy bread on the way.
Who ate the cake? (all of it)
I won't make it in time.

units.title: Ho, ju, ich · Him, her, them
units.intro: Short object words: ma me, ťa you, ho him/it, ju her/it, nás us, vás you all, ich them.
units.logic: They slip into second place in the sentence: Vidím ho, Zajtra ťa vyzdvihnem. After a preposition you need the long form: na mňa, pre teba. And ho/ju also mean "it" for masculine/feminine things: kľúč → mám ho.
units.fr: Same job as le, la, les, but the position follows the sentence, not the verb: Je le vois = Vidím ho.

items.en: I'll pick you up at six.
Where's the key? I don't have it.
Here it is. (handing over something feminine, e.g. a bag)
Say hi to them from me.

items.note: Helping is done "to" someone: mi, not ma.

units.title: Čí je to? · Whose
units.intro: My, your, his, her, our, and a word English doesn't have: svoj, "one's own".
units.logic: môj, tvoj, náš, váš agree with the thing owned, like adjectives: môj brat, moja sestra, moje auto. jeho, jej, ich never change. svoj replaces any of them when the owner is the subject: Vezmi si svoj kabát "take your (own) coat".
units.fr: môj, moja, moje = mon, ma… And svoj solves a French ambiguity: Il a pris son manteau (his own, or someone else's?). Vzal svoj kabát can only be his own.

items.en: Where is your hotel? (formal or to several)
Their kids are already grown up.
Our granny bakes the best cakes.

units.title: Ktorý · Who, which, that
units.intro: Joining two sentences into one: the man who lives here, the film that I wanted to see.
units.logic: ktorý / ktorá / ktoré agrees with the noun it points back to: muž, ktorý…, žena, ktorá…, dieťa, ktoré…. Questions inside sentences work the same way: Neviem, kde býva. There's always a comma before them.
units.fr: ktorý covers qui, que and lequel in one word, and the comma before it is compulsory.

items.sk: To je muž, ktorý tu býva.
items.en: That's the man who lives here.

items.sk: Žena, ktorá spieva, je moja teta.
items.en: The woman who's singing is my aunt.

items.sk: To je film, ktorý som chcela vidieť.
items.en: That's the film I wanted to see. (she says)
I don't know where he lives.

items.sk: Pamätáš si, kedy sme sa stretli?
items.en: Do you remember when we met?
I don't understand why he did it.

units.title: Detstvo · Childhood
units.intro: A2 means you can talk about your past: where you grew up, what you used to do. Slovaks love asking Kde si vyrastala?
units.logic: Habits in the past use the ongoing verb: Každé leto sme chodili k babke, "every summer we used to go to granny's". Slovak has no separate "used to": the ongoing verb does that job.
units.fr: That's the French imparfait: chodili sme = nous allions. And keď som bola malá = quand j'étais petite.

items.note: A man teacher is učiteľ.

items.en: Where did you grow up? (to a woman)
I grew up by the sea. (she says)

items.sk: Keď som bola malá, mala som psa.
items.en: When I was little, I had a dog. (she says)

items.sk: Každé leto sme chodili k babke.
items.en: Every summer we used to go to granny's.

items.note: hrať sa is playing as children do; hrať is playing a game or an instrument.

items.en: My best friend lived next door.
I was afraid of the dark. (she says)
items.note: Fear takes the "of" form: tma → bojím sa tmy.

items.en: I have fond memories of it. (she says)

units.title: Príroda · Nature & animals
units.intro: About two-fifths of Slovakia is forest. A free weekend often means ísť do prírody, "going out into nature".
units.logic: Baby animals get a cute ending, -iatko or -ätko, and are always neuter: mačka → mačiatko, pes → šteniatko, kôň → žriebätko.
units.fr: príroda = la nature, and ísť do prírody ≈ partir au vert.

items.note: Slovakia has over a thousand brown bears; in the mountains you'll see warning signs.

items.en: We went for a walk in the forest.

units.title: Pozvánky · Invitations & messages
units.intro: Inviting, accepting, saying no nicely, and signing off a card or a message.
units.logic: Invite with pozývam ťa na + the "thing you want" form: na kávu, na večeru, na oslavu. To say no nicely: Žiaľ, nemôžem, then a reason with lebo.
units.fr: S pozdravom = Cordialement, Drahá teta = Chère tante, and Bozkávam = Bisous.

items.en: Let me take you out for a coffee.

variants.en: I'm inviting you to a party.

items.en: Let me know. / Get in touch.

items.note: For colleagues and strangers. Family gets Bozkávam.

units.title: Technika · Tech trouble
units.intro: Phones, wifi, and things that stop working: everyday tech talk.
units.logic: Pokazil sa mi telefón: in Slovak the phone "broke itself", and mi says who it happened to. Same pattern: vybila sa mi baterka, my battery died on me.
units.fr: Nefunguje to = ça ne marche pas. And the mi is the French me in mon téléphone m'a lâché.

units.title: Koľko? · How much, how many
units.intro: After amounts, Slovak switches to the "of" form: a bottle of wine, a lot of people.
units.logic: After veľa, málo, trochu, kilo, fľaša the noun takes the "of" form: fľaša vína, trochu cukru. Numbers: 2–4 keep the normal plural (tri deti), from 5 up it's the "of" form (päť detí, desať eur). In the plural it often just loses its ending: žena → päť žien.
units.fr: It's the French de after quantities: beaucoup de gens = veľa ľudí, une bouteille de vin = fľaša vína. Slovak puts the "of" into the ending.

items.en: There were a lot of people there.

units.title: Najprv, potom · Telling a story
units.intro: Small words that turn separate sentences into a story.
units.logic: Put the sequence word first; the little words sme, som, sa still come second: Najprv sme išli na obed. Potom sme sa prechádzali.
units.fr: najprv = d'abord, potom = ensuite, nakoniec = finalement, zrazu = tout à coup, kým = pendant que.

items.en: Then we went for a walk.
In the end we took a taxi home.
While I was cooking, Jakub was tidying up.
During the holiday I read a lot. (she says)
We've known each other since then.

units.title: Nikto, nič, nikdy · Nobody, nothing, never
units.intro: The some- and no- words: niekto / nikto, niečo / nič, niekde / nikde, niekedy / nikdy.
units.logic: Slovak doubles the negative, and it's correct: Nikto nič nevie, "nobody knows anything", literally "nobody nothing doesn't know". Every ni- word needs ne- on the verb.
units.fr: Like French ne… personne, ne… rien, ne… jamais, but Slovak can stack as many as it likes: Nikdy nikomu nič nehovorím.

items.note: The kind reply when someone apologises to you.

items.en: Sometimes I'm the one who cooks.
I've heard that somewhere before. (she says)

units.title: Prosím vás · Polite instructions
units.intro: Instructions for strangers, patients, and anyone you call vy.
units.logic: Take the ty command and add -te: počkaj → počkajte, povedz → povedzte, sadni si → sadnite si. For "don't", put ne- in front: nebojte sa.
units.fr: Just like attends → attendez: počkaj → počkajte. Even the ending sounds alike.

units.title: Krajiny a jazyky · Countries & languages
units.intro: Slovakia has five neighbours: Česko, Poľsko, Ukrajina, Maďarsko, Rakúsko. Slovaks and Czechs understand each other without translation.
units.logic: Most countries end in -sko and are neuter: Francúzsko; you go do Francúzska and live vo Francúzsku. Speaking a language uses po: po francúzsky, po nemecky. The language itself is a noun: francúzština, nemčina.
units.fr: The same three-way split as French: la France / le français / parler français = Francúzsko / francúzština / hovoriť po francúzsky.

items.note: One word for both, like French langue.
A man is cudzinec.

items.en: Have you ever been to France? (to a woman)
I understand Czech, but I don't speak it.

units.title: Povolania · Jobs
units.intro: What people do. Almost every Slovak job has a male and a female form: učiteľ / učiteľka, lekár / lekárka.
units.logic: The female form usually adds -ka: predavač → predavačka, kuchár → kuchárka. Some change a little more: právnik → právnička. To a child: Čím chceš byť?, "what do you want to be?"
units.fr: Like avocat / avocate, but Slovak does it for nearly every job, down to psychiatrička.

items.note: Like cousin Filip.
Also a title: pán inžinier, written Ing. before the name.

items.en: What do you do at work?
What do you want to be? (to a child)

units.title: V lekárni · At the pharmacy
units.intro: A Slovak pharmacy (lekáreň, look for the green cross) sells many medicines only over the counter, and the pharmacist will gladly advise you.
units.logic: Medicine for something is na + the "thing you want" form: niečo na kašeľ, tabletky na spanie. Against pain: proti bolesti.
units.fr: Máte niečo na kašeľ? = Vous avez quelque chose contre la toux ? And bez receptu = sans ordonnance.

items.en: Do you have something for a cough?

variants.en: Do you have something for a runny nose?

items.en: Is it available without a prescription?
How often should I take it?
Three times a day, after meals.
Are you allergic to anything? (to a woman)
Where's the duty pharmacy (open at night)?

units.title: Reakcie · Reacting like a Slovak
units.intro: Half of any conversation is reacting. These little phrases make you sound like you've lived here for years.
units.logic: Držím palce is literally "I'm holding thumbs": Slovaks tuck their thumbs into their fists for luck, where English crosses fingers.
units.fr: To je škoda = c'est dommage, nevadí = ce n'est pas grave, to snáď nie! = c'est pas vrai !

items.en: I'm glad you came. (she says, to a man)

units.title: Šport · Sport & keeping fit
units.intro: Ice hockey is close to a national religion: when Slovakia plays at the World Championship, the streets go quiet.
units.logic: Regular exercise often uses chodiť + a verb: chodím plávať, chodím behať, "I go swimming, I go running". A place takes do: chodím do posilňovne.
units.fr: Chodím plávať = je vais nager: the same "go + verb" as French.

items.note: Svalovica: the ache the day after exercise. English has no single word for it.

units.title: Kedy? · Time expressions
units.intro: When things happened, or will: a week ago, in an hour, next month.
units.logic: pred + time = ago: pred týždňom. o + time = in (from now): o hodinu. za + time = within: za dva dni. Something still going on uses the present + už: Učím sa už rok, "I've been learning for a year".
units.fr: pred týždňom = il y a une semaine, o hodinu = dans une heure, and učím sa už rok = j'apprends depuis un an, with the present, just like French.

items.en: I arrived an hour ago. (she says)
I'll be back in ten minutes.

items.sk: Ako dlho sa učíš po slovensky?
items.en: How long have you been learning Slovak?

items.sk: Učím sa po slovensky už rok.
items.en: I've been learning Slovak for a year now.
How long have you two known each other?
I'll get it done by Friday.

units.title: Rýchlo, pomaly · How you do things
units.intro: Words that say how: fast, slowly, often, well or badly, and how to compare them.
units.logic: From an adjective, swap the ending for -o or -e: rýchly → rýchlo, pekný → pekne. To compare, add -ejšie or -šie: rýchlejšie, pomalšie. The irregular ones: dobre → lepšie, zle → horšie, veľa → viac, málo → menej.
units.fr: -o / -e does the job of -ment: pomaly = lentement. And lepšie = mieux, viac = plus.

units.title: Vošla, vyšla · Which way
units.intro: One verb, ísť (to go), and a set of prefixes that point the way.
units.logic: prišla arrived · odišla left · vošla went in · vyšla went out or up · zišla came down · prešla went across · obišla went around · došla got as far as.
units.fr: Where French needs a new verb each time (entrer, sortir, monter, descendre, traverser), Slovak keeps ísť and swaps the prefix.

items.note: The east is where the sun "goes out".

items.en: We went down to the village.
We made it all the way to the top.
Shall we go for a walk?

units.title: Mala by si · Giving advice
units.intro: Should, had better, it would be better: advice for friends, and for patients.
units.logic: Mal by som / mala by som = I should: the past form + by, like "would". Mala by si viac spať, "you should sleep more". Firmer: radšej, "better": Radšej zostaň doma. No person at all: treba, "one needs to".
units.fr: Mala by si = tu devrais, radšej = plutôt / mieux vaut, bolo by lepšie = ce serait mieux, treba = il faut.

items.en: You should sleep more. (to a woman)

items.sk: Mal by si ísť k lekárovi.
items.en: You should see a doctor. (to a man)
You shouldn't drink so much. (to a man)
It would be better to wait.
You need to drink plenty of water.
There's no need to be afraid.
You don't have to do it right away.
If you like, I'll help you.

units.title: Slovenská kuchyňa · Food traditions
units.intro: Slovak cooking grew out of shepherd and farm life in the mountains: potatoes, cabbage and sheep's cheese. The national dish, bryndzové halušky, combines all three ideas. At Christmas almost every family serves kapustnica (sauerkraut soup) and fried kapor (carp), and the dinner opens with thin oblátky wafers spread with honey.

items.note: The national dish. Bryndza is a soft, salty sheep's cheese.
Many families keep the Christmas carp alive in the bathtub for a day or two before Christmas Eve.
Eaten with goose fat, poppy seeds or jam. Especially popular around St. Martin's Day in November.
Pressed into carved wooden moulds, so each one carries a pattern.
From the Orava region. Literally "little whip".

items.en: fried dough with garlic and cheese
Bryndzové halušky are the national dish.

items.sk: Na Štedrý večer jeme kapustnicu a kapra.
items.en: On Christmas Eve we eat sauerkraut soup and carp.
Oštiepok is a smoked sheep's cheese.

units.title: Ľudová kultúra · Folk traditions
units.intro: Slovak folk culture is still very alive: villages have their own kroj (costume), folk ensembles perform everywhere, and the shepherd's flute fujara is on UNESCO's list of intangible heritage. The best-known folk hero is Jánošík, an 18th-century outlaw who, legend says, took from the rich and gave to the poor.

items.note: Almost two metres long, played standing up. Its sound is deep and haunting.
A masculine noun ending in -a, because it's a man.
Travelling craftsmen who mended pots with wire. A symbol of the Kysuce region.
Masks, parades and pork feasts before Lent.

items.sk: Jánošík bral bohatým a dával chudobným.
items.en: Jánošík took from the rich and gave to the poor.
The fujara is on the UNESCO list.
In Čičmany the houses are painted.
items.note: Dark wooden houses covered with white geometric patterns, originally to protect the wood.

items.sk: Na svadbách sa tancuje do rána.
items.en: At weddings people dance until morning.

units.title: Krásy Slovenska · Places & nature
units.intro: For a small country, Slovakia packs in a lot: the High Tatras, over 6,000 caves, more castles and castle ruins per person than almost anywhere in Europe, and several UNESCO sites. Two of the best are right next to Spišská Nová Ves: Spišský hrad and the gorges of Slovenský raj.

items.sk: Gerlachovský štít je najvyšší vrch Karpát.
items.en: Gerlach Peak is the highest mountain in the Carpathians.

items.sk: Spišský hrad je jeden z najväčších hradov v strednej Európe.
items.en: Spiš Castle is one of the largest castles in Central Europe.

items.sk: Slovenský raj je blízko Spišskej Novej Vsi.
items.en: Slovak Paradise is near Spišská Nová Ves.
items.note: Gorges climbed with ladders and chains over waterfalls.

items.sk: Dobšinská ľadová jaskyňa je plná ľadu aj v lete.
items.en: The Dobšiná Ice Cave is full of ice even in summer.

items.sk: Banská Štiavnica bola bohatá vďaka striebru.
items.en: Banská Štiavnica grew rich thanks to silver.
The Váh is the longest Slovak river.

units.title: Slovensko dnes · Slovakia today
units.intro: Slovakia has about 5.4 million people, joined the EU and NATO in 2004, and has used the euro since 2009. The flag and coat of arms carry the double cross on three hills (the hills stand for the Tatra, Fatra and Mátra). The national anthem, Nad Tatrou sa blýska, means "Lightning over the Tatras". And when the national hockey team plays, the whole country stops.

items.en: Bratislava is the capital of Slovakia.

items.sk: Na Slovensku žije asi päť a pol milióna ľudí.
items.en: About five and a half million people live in Slovakia.

items.sk: Slovensko je v Európskej únii od roku 2004.
items.en: Slovakia has been in the EU since 2004.

items.sk: V roku 2002 sme vyhrali majstrovstvá sveta v hokeji.
items.en: In 2002 we won the ice hockey world championship.
items.note: Every Slovak over 30 remembers where they were.

items.en: Many Hungarians live in the south.
items.note: About 8% of the population. Revúca's region, Gemer, is one of the mixed areas.

units.title: Veľká Morava · Great Moravia
units.intro: Slavs settled the area around the 6th century. In the 9th century they formed Great Moravia, an early Slavic state. In 863 the brothers Cyril and Methodius came from Byzantium, created the first Slavic alphabet (hlaholika, Glagolitic) and translated the liturgy into Old Slavonic. Their feast day, 5 July, is a public holiday.

items.sk: Cyril a Metod prišli v roku 863.

items.en: They created the first Slavic script.

items.sk: Nitra je jedno z najstarších slovenských miest.
items.en: Nitra is one of the oldest Slovak towns.
items.note: Prince Pribina had the first known church in the region built there in the 9th century.

items.sk: Piaty júl je sviatok svätého Cyrila a Metoda.
items.en: July fifth is the feast of Saints Cyril and Methodius.

units.title: Uhorsko · The Kingdom of Hungary
units.intro: For about a thousand years, until 1918, today's Slovakia was part of the Kingdom of Hungary (Uhorsko). When the Ottomans took Buda, Bratislava (then called Prešporok or Pressburg) became the coronation city: between 1563 and 1830, 11 kings and 8 queens were crowned there, including Maria Theresa. In the 19th century Ľudovít Štúr and his friends laid the foundations of standard Slovak, the language she's learning now.

items.en: Bratislava used to be called Prešporok.
Hungarian kings were crowned in Bratislava.

items.sk: Mária Terézia bola korunovaná v Bratislave.
items.en: Maria Theresa was crowned in Bratislava.

items.sk: Ľudovít Štúr je otec spisovnej slovenčiny.
items.en: Ľudovít Štúr is the father of standard Slovak.

items.sk: Jánošík žil na začiatku osemnásteho storočia.
items.en: Jánošík lived at the beginning of the 18th century.

units.title: Československo · Czechoslovakia
units.intro: On 28 October 1918, after World War I, Slovaks and Czechs founded Czechoslovakia. Its co-founder Milan Rastislav Štefánik, an astronomer, general and diplomat, is a national hero. During World War II Slovaks rose against the fascist regime in the Slovak National Uprising (SNP) on 29 August 1944. From 1948 the country was communist. In 1968 the Slovak Alexander Dubček led the Prague Spring, "socialism with a human face", until Soviet tanks ended it.

items.sk: Štefánik bol astronóm, generál a diplomat.
items.en: Štefánik was an astronomer, a general and a diplomat.

items.sk: Dvadsiaty deviaty august je výročie SNP.
items.en: August twenty-ninth is the anniversary of the Slovak National Uprising.

items.sk: Dubček chcel socializmus s ľudskou tvárou.
items.en: Dubček wanted socialism with a human face.

units.title: Nežná revolúcia · Freedom & independence
units.intro: On 17 November 1989 student protests began the Velvet Revolution, which Slovaks call Nežná revolúcia, "the gentle revolution". Crowds filled the squares jingling their keys: time for the communists to go. Three years later Czechs and Slovaks split peacefully, and on 1 January 1993 the independent Slovak Republic was born. Jakub's parents grew up on both sides of this story.

items.sk: Sedemnásty november je Deň boja za slobodu a demokraciu.
items.en: November seventeenth is the Day of the Struggle for Freedom and Democracy.
People jingled their keys on the squares.
The Slovak Republic was founded on January first, 1993.
